Nevada Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Nevada house?

Check the statute and talk to a Nevada attorney about your facts.

Do squatters have rights to a house in Nevada?

A squatter has no automatic right to a Nevada house. Title can pass by adverse possession only after a long, open and continuous claim that meets several statutes at once, and an unauthorized occupant can be removed through a court process the law spells out.

People use the word squatter for very different situations: someone who walked into a vacant house, a former tenant who stayed after a lease ended, an heir living in a parent's home, or a person who was let in by a fake landlord. Nevada treats these differently. A tenant who stays after notice falls under the landlord-tenant chapters, while a person who never had permission is handled as an unlawful or unauthorized occupant.

For a seller, the first question is which of these you are dealing with, because it decides the notice and the court.

What does it take to win title by adverse possession in Nevada?

The claimant has to meet requirements in more than one section of NRS chapter 11, and tax payment is one that many people overlook.

  • Five years of occupation. NRS 11.150 requires, in addition to the requirements of NRS 11.120 or 11.140, that the land was occupied and claimed for 5 years, continuously.
  • Payment of taxes. The same section requires that the claimant or predecessors paid all state, county and municipal taxes levied and assessed for that period, or tendered payment.
  • Possession in a recognized form. For a claim not founded on a written instrument, NRS 11.140 deems land possessed only when it has been protected by a substantial enclosure or has been usually cultivated or improved.

NRS 11.070 supports the five year frame from the owner's side. It says no cause of action founded on title to real property is effective unless the party or a predecessor was seized or possessed of the premises within 5 years before the act in question. An owner who pays the tax and keeps watch over the property makes the claimant's job much harder, because the claimant must show the taxes were paid or tendered.

None of this is easy to meet for someone who simply moved into a vacant house last month. Still, a claim can cloud title, and a clouded title is hard to sell.

How can an owner remove an unauthorized occupant in Nevada?

Use the court. The Civil Law Self-Help Center, a Clark County nonprofit legal service, describes a civil removal process that an owner can use whether or not anyone has been arrested, built around a 4 day notice to surrender.

StepWhat the Self-Help Center describes
1. Notice to SurrenderA 4 judicial day notice, which does not count the day of service, Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays or holidays
2. ServicePersonally in front of a witness; or with a person of suitable age and discretion plus mailing; or posting plus mailing, in that order
3. Occupant respondsLeaves, or files an affidavit with a legal defense by the end of the fourth judicial day
4. Owner's complaintFiled with the Justice Court with the notice and proof of service attached; the Center lists a $71 filing fee
5. Court reviewA hearing within 7 judicial days if a defense is raised; otherwise a removal order, carried out by the constable or sheriff within 24 hours

The notice must name the court, tell the occupant about the right to oppose it by affidavit, warn that a summary order could lead to removal within 24 hours, and say that the owner will provide safe storage of belongings for 21 days at the occupant's cost. An occupant can ask the court for up to 20 more days to move, but only in the answer filed within the four day window.

When can an owner change the locks after an arrest?

NRS 40.412 gives an owner a faster route in one narrow case: all known unlawful or unauthorized adult occupants have been arrested for housebreaking or unlawful occupancy, and any minor occupants have been taken into State custody. Only then may the owner retake possession and change the locks.

The statute attaches strict conditions. At the time the locks are changed, the owner or an authorized representative must post a written notice on the dwelling that identifies the address, the court with jurisdiction, and the date possession was retaken. The notice stays posted at least 21 calendar days, and a copy goes to the court within 1 day after the locks change, with an address for service.

  • The occupant has 21 calendar days to contest by filing a verified complaint for reentry.
  • Reentry without a court order is a criminal offense, punishable by up to 4 years in prison.
  • The owner must provide safe storage of remaining personal property and can dispose of it after 21 calendar days unless the occupant files an affidavit under NRS 40.414.
  • The section does not apply if any unlawful or unauthorized occupant is still occupying the dwelling.

The last point is the one owners miss. If someone is still living there, this section does not authorize a lock change.

How is a tenant who stays different from a squatter?

A tenant is someone who entered with permission under a lease or agreement, and the notice rules differ. Under NRS 40.2516, a tenant who fails to perform a condition of the lease and does not comply within 5 days after written notice is guilty of an unlawful detainer, and the landlord may then seek possession under the summary eviction statutes.

That is a different clock and a different notice from the 4 judicial day surrender notice for an unauthorized occupant. Use the notice that matches the occupant's status. Our Nevada landlord tenant guide covers the tenant side.

When the occupant is a relative who has moved into an inherited house, or someone who says they were promised the property, treat it as a question for an attorney. Those claims sometimes rest on documents or payments, and the quick removal process is built for people with no right at all.

How does an occupied house affect a sale?

An occupied house can still sell, but the buyer needs a clear path to possession. A traditional buyer with a lender usually wants an appraisal, an inspection and a vacant property at closing, and an unauthorized occupant can stall every one of those steps.

Owners often have three questions at this point: who is living there, what paper they hold, and what the county shows as the owner of record. A look at the recorder's records and the treasurer's account tells you whether the tax is current, which matters because the five year tax requirement in NRS 11.150 works in the owner's favor when the owner has paid.

  1. Document the occupancy with photos, dates and any police report numbers.
  2. Keep the property taxes current, and keep the receipts.
  3. Choose the right notice, civil removal or tenant eviction, and serve it exactly as the court rules require.
  4. Do not turn off utilities, remove belongings or change locks outside NRS 40.412 without legal advice.

We buy Nevada houses as-is, including houses with occupants or damage left behind. If you are weighing a removal case against a direct sale, we can talk through both and look at your timeline without any obligation.

More questions about Nevada Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long does adverse possession take in Nevada?

The statute requires 5 years of continuous occupation and claim, plus payment of all taxes levied for that period, or a tender of payment (NRS 11.150). Possession must also meet NRS 11.140 if no written instrument is involved.

Can a squatter claim my Nevada house if I pay the property taxes?

The claimant must show that taxes for the 5 year period were paid by the claimant or predecessors, or tendered. If the owner paid them, that requirement is hard to meet (NRS 11.150).

Can I change the locks on an occupied Nevada house?

Not under NRS 40.412 while any unlawful or unauthorized occupant is still living there. The section applies only after all known adult occupants have been arrested and minors taken into State custody, and reentry without a court order can be a crime.

How fast can an unauthorized occupant be removed in Nevada?

After the 4 judicial day notice and a Justice Court complaint, the Civil Law Self-Help Center says the constable serves a removal order requiring the occupant to leave within 24 hours. A hearing may be set within 7 judicial days if the occupant raises a defense.

Who stores belongings left in the home after a Nevada removal?

The owner must provide safe storage for 21 days, and the occupant pays reasonable inventory, moving and storage costs before getting the property back (NRS 40.412; Civil Law Self-Help Center).

Nevada Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit or surety bond (including last month's rent) exceeding 3 months' periodic rent. (NRS 118A.242; source)
  • Rent may be increased only with written notice 60 days in advance of the first rental payment to be increased (30 days for periodic tenancies of less than 1 month). (NRS 118A.300; source)
  • NRS 118A.290 covers habitability of the dwelling unit and prohibits fees for repairs/maintenance that are the landlord's duty (title only). (NRS 118A.290; source)
  • NRS 118A.390 prohibits unlawful removal/exclusion of a tenant or willful interruption of essential services (self-help eviction). (NRS 118A.390; source)
Selling in Nevada?
We buy Nevada houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which Nevada laws cover a rented house?

NRS chapter 118A is the Nevada landlord and tenant statute for dwellings, and chapter 40 sets the court procedures for removing a tenant. Mobile home parks sit in a separate chapter, 118B, which this page does not cover.

Nevada's two chapters divide the work. Chapter 118A covers the rental agreement, deposits, rent increases, repairs and what each side owes. Chapter 40 covers notices to surrender and the summary eviction process after a tenant defaults or a tenancy ends.

A rental agreement cannot waive a tenant's rights under the chapter. NRS 118A.220 lists prohibited provisions, which include a tenant agreeing to give up rights or remedies, authorizing someone to confess judgment, or agreeing to pay the landlord's attorney's fees, other than a clause awarding reasonable fees to the prevailing party.

What happens to a tenant's lease when the owner sells?

The lease continues. NRS 118A.349 says that when the property is voluntarily sold, and unless the new owner and the tenant agree to change or end the lease, the new owner takes on the previous owner's rights and obligations under the rental agreement, and the tenant keeps the tenant's rights and obligations.

The new owner has to send the tenant a notice within 30 days after the sale. It must give the new owner's contact information for rent, say that the existing agreement continues through the tenancy, state the amount held as a security deposit, and warn that failing to pay rent to the new owner or follow the lease is a breach.

A seller with a tenant should plan for these points:

  • The buyer inherits a lease that may have months left, so rent, term and any renewal clauses belong in the sale paperwork.
  • The deposit must follow the property, which is covered in the next section.
  • If the buyer wants the house empty, an agreement with the tenant is the clean path. The statute leaves room for the new owner and tenant to modify or end the lease by agreement.

What must the seller do with the security deposit?

Before recording the deed, the landlord must either hand the remaining deposit to the buyer in writing or tell the buyer in writing that the deposit has been returned to the tenant. NRS 118A.244 sets that rule, and it says the successor must accept the deposit and may not demand an additional one during the term of the rental agreement.

When the landlord's interest ends by sale, the landlord must within a reasonable time do one of two things. The first is to notify the tenant in writing of the successor's name, address and telephone number and that the deposit balance was transferred. The second is to return the remaining deposit to the tenant. Either step relieves the landlord of further liability for the deposit.

Deposits carry real exposure for an owner who skips this. A landlord who fails to return the remainder within 30 days after a tenancy ends is liable for damages in an amount equal to the entire deposit, plus a further sum the court fixes of up to the amount of the deposit under NRS 118A.242.

Which numbers does a Nevada landlord have to know?

Several limits come straight from the statute, and they matter in a sale because a buyer's lawyer will check each one. This table collects the main ones from chapter 118A.

TopicRuleStatute
Security deposit cap3 months' periodic rent, including last month's rentNRS 118A.242
Return of depositItemized accounting and remainder within 30 days after the tenancy endsNRS 118A.242
Rent increase notice60 days written notice (30 days for periodic tenancies under 1 month)NRS 118A.300
Late feeNot before 3 calendar days after the due date, and no more than 5 percent of periodic rentNRS 118A.210
Landlord entryAt least 24 hours notice, at reasonable times, except in an emergencyNRS 118A.330
Cure period for habitability or lease breach by landlord14 days after written noticeNRS 118A.350, 118A.355
Unlawful lockout or utility shutoffActual damages or up to $2,500 fixed by the court, or bothNRS 118A.390

Can an owner show the house to buyers while a tenant lives there?

Yes, with notice. NRS 118A.330 says a tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for the landlord to enter to exhibit the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, among other purposes. The landlord must give at least 24 hours' notice of the intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times during normal business hours, unless the tenant agrees to shorter notice or to entry outside business hours.

Emergencies are the exception, and a landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

Put the showing schedule in writing and keep it modest, since the 24 hour rule applies to each entry.

How can a landlord end a tenancy before selling?

Only through the notice and court steps the statutes set out, and the notice depends on the type of tenancy and the reason. NRS 40.251 says a tenant in a dwelling under chapter 118A is guilty of unlawful detainer after the lease term ends or is terminated and a notice period expires, which is at least 7 days for week-to-week tenancies and at least 30 days for other periodic tenancies. A 5 day notice applies where the tenant failed to perform basic or contractual obligations under chapter 118A.

For unpaid rent, NRS 40.253 provides a written notice requiring payment or surrender by the close of business on the seventh judicial day after service. Under NRS 40.2516, a tenant who fails to perform another lease condition after written notice has 5 days to comply or leave.

Notices must be served by the methods in NRS 40.280, which include delivery by the sheriff, a constable, a licensed process server or an attorney's agent. A fixed-term lease does not simply end because the owner lists the house, and NRS 118A.349 confirms the lease follows the property.

What is a landlord not allowed to do?

A landlord may not take back possession by self-help. NRS 118A.480 says possession may be recovered only through an action for possession or similar proceeding, when the tenant surrenders, or when the tenant abandons the unit. NRS 118A.390 adds that unlawfully removing a tenant, blocking entry or willfully cutting essential services gives the tenant a right to recover possession, actual damages, or an amount of up to $2,500 fixed by the court.

A tenant may file a verified complaint for expedited relief within 5 judicial days after the unlawful act.

Property left behind is handled by NRS 118A.460. The landlord must provide safe storage for 30 days after abandonment or eviction, and may charge reasonable costs of inventory, moving and storage. After that period, the landlord may dispose of the property if there were reasonable efforts to find the tenant, written notice of intent to dispose, and 14 days have passed since the notice. NRS 118A.520 abolishes distraint for rent.

What can a tenant demand when the house needs repairs?

A dwelling must be habitable at all times, and NRS 118A.290 defines habitability by reference to housing and health codes and to basics such as weatherproof roof and walls, working plumbing, water supply, heating and electrical systems. A landlord also may not charge fees for repairs or maintenance that are the landlord's own duty.

The tenant's remedies are staged. After written notice, the landlord has 14 days to fix a remediable failure or make best efforts. If the landlord does not, the tenant may end the lease, recover actual damages, ask the court for relief, or under NRS 118A.355 withhold rent without late fees until the problem is remedied or a good faith attempt is made. For small repairs where the cost is less than $100 or one month's rent, whichever is greater, NRS 118A.360 lets a tenant who has notified the landlord make the repair and deduct the reasonable cost from rent, up to that amount.

A tenant cannot use these remedies for conditions the tenant or a guest caused. Keep written records of repair requests and fixes, since a buyer will ask for them.

What if the seller stays in the house after closing?

A person who sold the property and keeps living there can be removed after a 3-day written notice to surrender, once title under the sale has been perfected. NRS 40.255 lists sale by the person, or by someone the person claims under, among the cases where holdover can be removed through the court procedures in NRS 40.290 to 40.420.

That matters to sellers who want a short rent-back after a cash sale. Put the rent-back in a written agreement with a clear end date, rent amount and deposit, because the statute treats the occupant as a holdover if the arrangement ends and the person stays.

More questions about Nevada Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

Does a Nevada tenant have to move when the owner sells the house?

No. NRS 118A.349 says the lease continues with the new owner unless the new owner and the tenant agree to change or end it. The new owner must send the tenant a notice within 30 days after the sale.

How much can a Nevada landlord charge for a security deposit?

The total of a security deposit and surety bond, including last month's rent, cannot exceed 3 months' periodic rent under NRS 118A.242. The landlord must return the remainder with an itemized accounting within 30 days after the tenancy ends.

How much notice must a Nevada landlord give before raising rent?

Written notice 60 days before the first rental payment to be increased, or 30 days for a periodic tenancy of less than one month, under NRS 118A.300.

How long does an eviction notice take for unpaid rent in Nevada?

NRS 40.253 provides a written notice to pay or surrender by the close of business on the seventh judicial day after service. A shorter period applies to certain weekly tenancies of no more than 45 days. The case then goes through the court.

Can a landlord change the locks or shut off utilities to clear a house for sale?

No. NRS 118A.480 requires a court process or a surrender or abandonment, and NRS 118A.390 lets a tenant recover possession, actual damages, or up to $2,500 as fixed by the court if the landlord locks out the tenant or interrupts essential services.

Who gets the security deposit when a rental is sold?

The seller must transfer the remaining deposit to the buyer in writing before recording the deed, or tell the buyer in writing that it was returned to the tenant, under NRS 118A.244. The buyer must accept the deposit and cannot demand an additional one during the lease term.
